source: Garivier & Moulines (2008) On upper-confidence bound policies for non-stationary bandit problems
finding: Bandit with reward distributions that change at unknown times. Two fixes: discount old data (D-UCB) or use only the last tau plays (SW-UCB). Both match a lower bound up to a log factor.
numbers: With a fixed number of breakpoints, D-UCB with discount 1-(4B)^-1*sqrt(Upsilon/T) has regret O(sqrt(T) log T). If breakpoints grow as T^alpha, regret is O(T^((1+alpha)/2) log T). SW-UCB with window tau = 2B*sqrt(T log T / Upsilon) gives the same order.
limits: Theory plus simulation for bounded rewards; needs the window or discount tuned to how often change happens (knowing Upsilon). It is UCB, not Thompson sampling.
agent_relevance: The class table should forget: weight recent runs more (window or discount). The best window shrinks as change gets more frequent, so the window is a setting to tune on our logs.

source: Russo, Van Roy, Kazerouni, Osband, Wen (2018) A tutorial on Thompson sampling
finding: Standard Thompson sampling stops exploring as the posterior sharpens, so it fails after drift. Two cheap fixes: use only the last tau observations, or inject uncertainty each step (Beta update that decays toward the prior).
numbers: Section 6.3 simulation: decay rate gamma=0.01, Bernoulli bandit, 10,000 runs each. Nonstationary TS keeps reasonable regret; plain TS degrades as the system drifts. Prior and stationary beta(1,1).
quote: With minor modification, TS remains an effective approach so long as model parameters change little over durations that are sufficient to identify effective actions.
limits: Simulated Bernoulli bandit only. The authors say that under nonstationarity no algorithm can promise regret that vanishes with time.
agent_relevance: For the class table use a Beta posterior per (class, mode) that decays toward the prior each step. One setting (gamma) replaces a separate change-detection module. Test gamma on a shifted log replay.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: The best way to spend test-time compute depends on question difficulty, and difficulty can serve as one cheap class feature. Questions go into five bins by the base model's own pass@1. Choosing the best strategy per bin beats best-of-N with about 4x less compute.
numbers: Bins from pass@1 over 2048 samples per question (MATH, PaLM 2-S*). Per-bin strategy picked with 2-fold cross validation. Compute-optimal beats best-of-N at roughly 4x less compute for revisions and search. Model-defined bins predicted compute efficacy better than hand-labelled MATH levels.
quote: difficulty acts as a sufficient statistic of a question when designing the compute-optimal strategy
limits: The difficulty estimate costs 2048 samples per question and the paper does not count that cost; the authors call it an exploration cost left for future work. Maths only. Model-predicted difficulty uses a learned verifier.
agent_relevance: Strong support for a difficulty class feature, with a warning: the cost of estimating it must be charged to the table. Our version can take difficulty from the running pass rate of the class, which costs nothing extra. Partial answer to gaps 2 and 7.

source: Snell et al. (2024) same paper, search by difficulty bin
finding: Which method is better flips with difficulty. On easy questions (levels 1-2) beam search against the process reward model gets worse as budget grows, while on levels 3-4 it beats best-of-N. On level 5 no method makes much progress.
numbers: Beam width 4 vs best-of-N, MATH, increasing generation budget. Easy bins: beam search degrades with budget. Bins 3-4: beam search consistently better. Level 5: little gain from any method.
limits: One model family and one verifier; the authors link the easy-bin loss to over-optimising the verifier. Not a short-vs-long mode test.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that the best mode depends on class: a global heavy mode loses on easy items. Gap 7 still needs the per-class, per-budget table on our tasks; this paper gives the shape only.

source: Zhang, Wisniewski, Tomeh, Charnois (2025) Reasoning strategies in LLMs: can they follow, prefer, and optimize
finding: How the oracle in the 47.2 vs 82.9 gap is built: it is the share of problems solved by at least one of the strategy-specific prompts, so any lucky sample counts.
numbers: Table 2: TruthQuest Phi-4 no strategy 47.2, oracle 82.9; R1-Distill 63.4 vs 90.1; ZebraLogic Phi-4 27.3 vs 37.7; Qwen3 32.0 vs 36.4. The four strategy prompts all land 45.1-49.0 on Phi-4 TruthQuest. Tables 10-11 report std over the 4 no-strategy samples per question.
limits: The paper does not report a control with the same number of samples of one prompt, so how much of 82.9 is pure sampling is not measured. Sampling at temperature 0.6, top-p 0.9.
agent_relevance: Do not read the oracle gap as predictable signal. Our test for gap 6 is the any-of-k of one fixed mode against the oracle over k modes, with repeated runs per item.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) same paper, difficulty split
finding: Selection gains are largest on easy items and small on hard ones, because the room for gain (oracle minus single) is smaller on hard items. Verifier-based picking helps in simple settings and fails on longer chains.
numbers: TruthQuest Phi-4 by number of characters (3 to 6): single strategy 65.7 / 49.7 / 40.5 / 33.5, average 47.2; verifier average 57.3; majority vote 54.9. ZebraLogic Phi-4: easy 58.6, hard 15.1; merged methods on hard 11.4-12.6 vs 12.5 single.
limits: Difficulty proxies are hand-made (character count, grid size). One dataset family; models of 14B scale or less.
agent_relevance: Item size is a usable cheap feature in puzzles. Where the single-mode ceiling is low and the oracle gap small, the table should not spend tokens on selection. Partial answer to gap 6: some of the gap is predictable by size; the rest is untested.

source: Brown, Juravsky, Ehrlich, Clark, Le, Re, Mirhoseini (2024) Large language monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: With many samples from the same prompt, coverage (any sample correct) rises almost log-linearly. So an any-of-k oracle rises with k even with no strategy difference. This is the noise baseline against which a strategy oracle must be compared.
numbers: MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000. SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250. Majority vote or reward model only moved from 40.50% to 41.41% over 100 to 10,000 samples.
quote: coverage growing nearly log-linearly with the number of samples over several orders of magnitude
limits: Coverage turns into accuracy only with a verifier; common verifiers plateau. Benchmarks are maths and code, not our tasks.
agent_relevance: Answers part of gap 6: a five-prompt oracle gains from sampling alone. Verification is the limiter, which fits G4 and G5. Control run needed: any-of-k of one mode vs any-of-k across k modes.

source: Chen, Xu, Liang et al. (2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Long reasoning models waste tokens on easy items. For 2+3 they use 1,953% more tokens than a conventional model. In over 92% of cases the first solution round is already correct, and it uses under 60% of total tokens.
numbers: QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1 on ASDIV and MATH500: first-round correct 89-97% by model and set (read from a figure); first round on ASDIV averages 287 tokens, 38.7% of the response. Their self-training cuts tokens 48.6% on MATH500 at the same accuracy.
limits: Mostly maths; two open reasoning models; the fix is training, not routing. Some percentages read from a figure.
agent_relevance: Evidence at the easy end for gap 7: the short mode is enough for easy classes, so a table with a cheap default should win there. The per-class pass rate at three budgets on our tasks is still missing.

source: Zhang, Zhang, Xiang, Cai (2026) Reasoning is not free: robust adaptive cost-efficient routing for LLM-as-a-judge (RACER)
finding: The token price lambda can be learned instead of fixed. A Lagrange multiplier is updated by primal-dual steps to meet a compute budget. It grows under tight budgets and falls toward zero when the budget is loose and the constraint stops binding.
numbers: Budgets C in {2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 5, 7, 10} (cost relative to instruct mode = 1), 20 repeats per budget; Appendix C.1 shows curves of reward, realized cost and lambda. At C=4, 10 replications over 3 test sets, RACER beats RouterBench-KNN, RouteLLM-MF and M-IRT by 0.64, 1.10 and 1.06 points (1.7B, 4B, 8B).
quote: the Lagrange multiplier dynamically adapts to the tightness of the compute budget
limits: Judge tasks, Qwen3 and Llama-3.1-8B; the router is a four-layer network on embeddings, not a code table. One author group; preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 4, in form: do not fix lambda by hand; make it a dual variable that rises until runs meet the token budget. In a code table it is one scalar update per batch. Not yet tested against the best fixed budget.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) RACER, sensitivity table
finding: Results are nearly flat across the second hyperparameter (a regularizer weight; its symbol was lost in text extraction). The budget, not that weight, sets the outcome.
numbers: Table 3, Qwen3-4B pair: accuracy 84.8-86.8 and cost 1.9-3.8 across settings at C=2, 3, 4. For C=3, 86.7 at cost 2.9 for two different settings.
limits: Identity of the parameter is uncertain from the extracted text; one model pair.
agent_relevance: A small sign that a budget-set price is not fragile. It does not test match to the best fixed budget, so gap 4 stays open.

source: Yang, Hou, Wei, Bao, Chang (2026) ARES: adaptive reasoning effort selection, normalised cost and gpt-oss-120b
finding: Reward design matters for per-class choice. Without normalising the cost penalty the router uses medium effort less after about 80 training steps in Airline, where medium is the best fixed level. With normalisation its share rises. On a stronger backbone ARES stays near High with fewer tokens.
numbers: Table 5, TAU-Bench Retail, gpt-oss-120b: Low 49.4, Medium 62.0, High 67.8 (558k tokens), ARES 65.2 (428k tokens), about 23% fewer tokens. First backbone Retail: ARES 54.8 = High; GPT-5 router 14.8 points lower.
limits: GRPO-trained router; Airline test is about 50 tasks (from earlier lines); the penalty form is tuned. Not a class table. ARES loses 2.6 points to High on gpt-oss-120b, so equal quality is not guaranteed.
agent_relevance: Shows the short mode wins on one class (Airline) and that a naive cost penalty hides it. Our table must score pass minus lambda*tokens per class and compare with every fixed budget. Gap 7: shape only, not our classes.

finding: Not found. The web search quota was exhausted in this run and I did not search through other services. No independent replication was found or ruled out.
numbers: 0 outside-lab replications found. Earlier lines a01-a12 remain one lab, plus Rieskamp 2008 (b04-b05) as an outside reanalysis.

source: Garivier & Moulines (2008) remarks on window size
finding: If there is no breakpoint, the best window is as large as possible. With more breakpoints the best window is smaller. So the runs per class needed before the table beats a global mode depend on how fast classes change.
numbers: Remarks 9 and 11: window tau ~ 2B*sqrt(T log T / Upsilon); with Upsilon = 0 take the largest window.
limits: Asymptotic orders with unknown constants; gives no sample count for small tables.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 gets a rule shape, not a count. Measure it by replaying logs with n runs per class (for example n=5, 10, 20, 50) and comparing with the global mode.

source: Snell et al. (2024) cost of difficulty estimation
finding: Two ways to get difficulty: oracle difficulty (ground-truth checks) and model-predicted difficulty (verifier scores). Both use 2048 samples per question, and neither cost is counted in the comparison.
numbers: 2048 samples per question for both estimates. The authors say balancing the compute spent assessing difficulty against applying the best approach is an exploration-exploitation trade-off left for future work.
limits: Cost accounting is missing, so the 4x saving is optimistic.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a class feature must be near-free. Use features known before running (size, task type, source) and learn difficulty from running logs, not from fresh sampling.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) strategy prompts vs no strategy
finding: Telling the model which strategy to use does not raise accuracy; with no prompt the model is as good as any named strategy. The strategy label is not the lever.
numbers: Phi-4 TruthQuest: no strategy 47.2, four strategy prompts 45.1-49.0; R1-Distill 63.4 vs 61.4-63.0; ZebraLogic Phi-4 27.3 vs 25.1-27.0; Qwen3 32.0 vs 31.0-32.0. Strategy-following annotated on 100 answers per model.
agent_relevance: Modes in the table should differ in cost or tools (token budget, sample count, tool use), not in a named reasoning style, since style prompts add little.
